actions.diff:
--- a/base58/__init__.py
+++ b/base58/__init__.py
@@ -43,6 +43,15 @@
-    string = b""
-    base = len(alphabet)
-    while i:
-        i, idx = divmod(i, base)
-        string = alphabet[idx:idx+1] + string
-    return string
+    string = bytearray()
+    base = len(alphabet)
+    # Peel 5 digits per big-int division; 58**5 fits a single 30-bit
+    # internal digit, so each remainder is split with small-int arithmetic.
+    chunk_base = base ** 5
+    while i >= chunk_base:
+        i, rem = divmod(i, chunk_base)
+        for _ in range(5):
+            rem, idx = divmod(rem, base)
+            string.append(alphabet[idx])
+    while i:
+        i, idx = divmod(i, base)
+        string.append(alphabet[idx])
+    string.reverse()
+    return bytes(string)

actions.reason: b58encode_int did one big-int divmod per output character and prepended to an immutable bytes object each time, so a fresh copy was made per digit. It now divides by base**5, which fits a single 30-bit internal int digit for base 58. Each remainder is split into 5 characters with small-int divmods, and the per-digit loop handles only the final high part, so no spurious leading digits appear. Characters are appended to a bytearray, which is reversed once and converted to bytes at the end. Output is unchanged for any alphabet length (equivalence harness: identical). Measured: check_ir 0.9508, encode_ir 0.8724, encode_long_ir 0.4346, int_ir 0.8866; decode metrics neutral (1.0001/1.0002).

journal.text:
Why does b58encode_int in base58/__init__.py do one big-int divmod per output character and prepend to an immutable bytes object each time? It does not need to. I replaced lines 43-48 (6 lines became 15). It now divides by base**5, which fits one 30-bit internal int digit for base 58. It splits each remainder into 5 characters with small-int divmods. The per-digit loop only handles the final high part, so no spurious leading digits.

The sandbox run on check_ir was accepted. Equivalence: identical outputs. Guard: ok, 1 files, 15 lines. check_ir ratio 0.9508. encode_ir ratio 0.8724. encode_long_ir went from 2905032739 to 1262542660, ratio 0.4346. int_ir ratio 0.8866. decode_ir 1.0001, decode_long_ir 1.0002, unchanged as expected.

I believe the encode path was dominated by per-digit big-int work and bytes copies. The gain grows with input length. The candidate is committed and waiting on independent replays. No verdict yet.

Next I want to look at whether b58decode_int has a similar per-character big-int cost. No numbers yet. I am least sure the high-part loop handles leading-zero edge cases beyond what the equivalence suite covers.
